text: — What Cvetko told — said the shy Ilcho, — that’s a later matter, but I know that Bay Ganyo had come to Prague earlier, had stayed there a long time, and had sold quite a lot of rose oil. Would you like me to tell you about it?
— If it’s about Bay Ganyo, don’t ask, just tell it! — we replied.

— Good. Listen then. Bay Ganyo arrives from Vienna in Prague. He gets off at the station, slings his saddlebags over his shoulder, and goes out into the street. The cabmen rush up to offer him their services — he nods to them that he does not want them. They take his gesture as affirmative, and a cab pulls up in front of him. Bay Ganyo gets angry, stares, and makes irritated gestures. The policeman notices this and orders the cabs to withdraw. Bay Ganyo wonders from whom he can find out where Jireček, our historian, lives. Jireček lived in Bulgaria, loves the Bulgarians, Bay Ganyo will go to him: “Good day” — “God grant you good” — and he may invite him into his house; why should he spend his money on hotels? While he is thinking thus, a porter with a red cap steps in front of him and offers to carry his saddlebags. Bay Ganyo asks him whether he knows where Jireček lives; the porter answers in the negative, but gives hope that it can be found, and again stretches out his hands to take the saddlebags. Bay Ganyo does not give them to him, first because the flasks are inside and he might “take off somewhere,” and second because he sees that he is well dressed, and who knows how much he will fleece him.

— Your grace, go ahead, I’ll follow you — says Bay Ganyo politely. — Leave the saddlebags; I’ll carry them. Bay Ganyo shows this politeness with calculation: he will both put the porter at ease and show him that he is not some great and rich man, so that the other one won’t think of fleecing him.

They go around asking at the crossroads where Jireček lives; at last someone remembered that the question was about Professor Jireček, told them whom to ask, they asked, and they found him. Bay Ganyo says to the porter a “be well, thank you” and enters Jireček’s lodgings.

— Oh! Good day, Mr. Yirechek, how are you, are you well? — exclaims Bay Ganyo in a most friendly tone as soon as he enters the host’s office. The latter extends his hand in surprise, invites him to sit down, and is annoyed with his memory, which does not remind him who this courteous friend is.

— Don’t you recognize me? — Bay Ganyo reminds him, mixing “you” formal and “you” informal. — Weren’t you a minister in Sofia? — Yes. — Well, I’m from there too! — Bay Ganyo concludes triumphantly. — That’s what you call compatriots, heh, heh, heh, of course! Do you remember the article in the newspaper “Slavyanin”?
— Yes, yes, I remember — replies Jireček in a restrained, condescending tone.

— Wow, they really dirtied you up!... But you just enjoy yourself, don’t worry about it at all! How much I’ve praised you!... They say Jireček is this, Jireček is that. — “Excuse me,” I say, “that’s not so.”

Irechek knows the Bulgarians well and therefore is not at all surprised by Bay Ganyo’s familiarity. The conversation continues for several minutes in this tone, then moves onto more practical ground: Bay Ganyo praises the landlord’s apartment, hints to him quite pointedly that “at last there is room for even one more strange fellow to settle in here,” talks to him about the hospitality of the Bulgarians, and expresses regret that “look, the others are not like us Bulgarians; if a foreigner enters a Bulgarian house, they will feed him, give him drink, and make up a bed for him.”

Irechek tries to impress upon him that the apartment is too small for his household. Bay Ganyo pretends not to hear and develops the theme of Bulgarian hospitality. From this theme, the conversation turns to Bay Ganyo’s little trade. He informs the host that he has brought rose oil for sale and declares to him: “Tomorrow, if you like, take me to all the factories; I agree. You’ll interpret for me, since I don’t know the language, right?”

Irechek hastens to reply that he is not acquainted with the manufacturers of essential oils, since his pursuits are of an entirely different kind, and besides, he has no free time; but he will tell him where the Bulgarian students gather, so that among them someone may be able to help him.

— If you like, sanquim — adds Bay Ganyo — I won’t overburden you. I’ll give the lady too (is she here?) a muskal of oil. I know her as well, of course (Ireček cannot stop wondering which lady is meant). And if you have relatives or friends here, tell them that I’ve brought oil — there’s no shame in that! I’ll be coming around you more often, and we’ll talk about Bulgaria. And if you please, I’m willing to stay at your place while I’m in Prague. Eh?
— Excuse me, but...
— I say, you know, if you please — explains Bay Ganyo, all tangled up, — it’s better for me at the hotel too, but come on, I thought, Jireček — he’s our man...
— Thank you for your attention; I would gladly keep you at home, but I do not have any spare rooms. Today, however, you are our guest and will have lunch with us.
— Let’s have lunch, why shouldn’t we have lunch! — agrees Bay Ganyo. — And your honor, so to speak, if not from my table, then from a Bulgarian one you have surely eaten.

Irechek is occupied with an urgent task, which is interrupted by the entrance of Bay Ganyo. The host sits as if on thorns and does not know how, in a delicate manner, to temporarily send off his loquacious guest. He rings the bell; a servant appears, whom he orders to inform the family that a guest from Bulgaria has arrived. Shortly afterward his mother enters. Bay Ganyo barely rises from his chair, makes a double gesture with his hand toward his forehead, and condescendingly says: “Oh, hello, well and good, let’s shake hands, just like that, in the Bulgarian way. How are you still? I’m glad.”
The lady greeted him kindly and, with a whole series of questions, showed lively interest in the guest’s homeland.
— Well, now tell the truth — asks Bay Ganyo, — where is it nicer, in Prague or in Sofia?

The lady is at a loss; she has not been in Sofia, and Bay Ganyo, at this question, glances at Jireček with a devilish smile, as if he wants to impress upon him his own view of women: “Well, she’s a woman, isn’t she? What’s there to talk to her about?…”

— His Grace will have lunch at home today — Irchek turns to his mother and then, so that he can continue his work, asks her in German to take Bay Ganyo into another room. The lady предлагает Bay Ganyo that they move to the adjoining room. Bay Ganyo looks at Irchek keenly, then at the saddlebags with the muskals, and calculates with his eyebrows: “They said something in German, who knows! But I don’t believe it. After all, he has been a minister in our country. Well, ministers aren’t much good either! But I don’t believe that about him.” — and then he rises uncertainly and follows the lady’s direction toward the adjoining room, but when he reaches the door, he turns around and tries to read in the hosts’ faces their intention, and notices several silent signs that the household members were indeed exchanging at that moment; these signs meant: “See that you keep him occupied for a longer time, because I have very urgent work,” but Bay Ganyo interpreted them differently.
— These things here may be bothering you — he says, indicating the saddlebags with his eyes.
— Oh, not at all. Please, don’t worry — replies Jireček.

— But they’ll still be bothering you, I know. Wait, let me take them into the other room — and she reaches out to take them, but the family politely resists. — As if I’m afraid, no, it’s just that, I said...

They pass into the reception room, and the lady closes the door behind her so that the noise from the office cannot be heard. She tries in every way to occupy Bay Ganyo with something interesting: she offers him various albums, shows him pictures, lays before him a whole pile of illustrations, but Bay Ganyo’s mind is quite elsewhere, and to the lady’s courtesies he replies with feigned indifference:

— I don’t want to, thank you: you look at them. I’ve looked at such pictures and portraits plenty of times! Don’t think that because I’m young I haven’t!

Bai Ganyo glances impatiently at his huge silver watch and begins a very interesting and timely conversation:

— I am very curious to study Europe. For example, let us say that at home noon comes — people sit down to lunch. With you it is arranged differently. When do you have lunch, for example?
— We usually have lunch at 5 o’clock, but today we can have lunch earlier too. Excuse me, I’ll leave you for just a minute — said the lady and went out through the other door.

Bay Ganyo sits alone in the salon, staring absentmindedly at the paintings, spitting on the carpet now and then (not because he is hungry, but who knows!), rubbing it with his boots, and listening intently at the slightest noise from the study. At one point he hears Jireček get up from his chair, take a few steps, and stop. “Damn it, I’m a fool too—why didn’t I bring my saddle-bags into this room?” Bay Ganyo sits on pins and needles; at last he cannot bear it, gets up, tiptoes across the carpet to the study door, bends his ear to the keyhole, and listens; he hears only his own frequent breathing and the pounding of blood in his ears. But even here Bay Ganyo does not calm down; he sees nothing through the keyhole, and, hesitantly pressing the door handle, opens it, pokes his head mysteriously into the study, and sees Jireček crouched down near his saddle-bags in front of a bookcase.

Bay Ganyo grins at him:

— Hee, hee, hee, are you working, are you working? Hee, hee, hee! Wait, I said, let me peek in. Go on working, it’s nothing, I’ll close it again.

Irechek looks at him in astonishment, without it crossing his mind what the reason for this peculiar curiosity might be.

Lunch is ready. They go into the dining room and sit around the table: Irechek’s parents, his sister, Bay Ganyo, and he himself. Before the meal begins, Bay Ganyo starts making the sign of the cross, while smiling, thereby wanting to show the hosts that he is not one of those simple folk and that he does not really believe that much, but still it is not a bad thing (we are on good terms with the devil; why not also burn a little incense to the Lord—in case of need).

— I’m a liberal, from the Liberal Party — he explains, — but now and then I make the sign of the cross; it’s not a bad thing, we’re only human... What is this, is it soup? Ah, I like soup. Chorba is a Turkish dish. And nowadays we eat more soup. Ah, pardon, excuse me, I’ve soiled your bundle... Tsk... tsk... tsk... Damn it!...

Eager to recommend himself as a civilized man, Bay Ganyo was unable to take the plate of soup that the hostess handed him straight, and spilled quite a bit of it onto the table; and before they could stop him, he gathered some of it with the spoon and poured it into his own plate. The hostess did not want to let him eat that soup, but out of delicacy he shielded his plate with his hands and did not want it to be changed.

— I have peppers in my saddlebags — Bay Ganyo announced unexpectedly. He was burning with the desire to rub one of the little peppers into the soup, which seemed quite bland for his stomach, but he was embarrassed to take out the peppers, lest they think him a boor, so he wanted first to sound out the hosts.
— Yes? Do you have peppers? — Irechek called out.

— How not, I’ve brought peppers with me; you know, “Dear Mother Bulgaria” can’t do without something spicy — says Bay Ganyo ironically, and without waiting any longer, he jumps up from the chair, goes down into the office, drags in his saddlebags, squats over them with his back to the hosts, and brings two peppers to the table.

— Two are enough for the five of us; they’re terribly hot — he says, shaking half a pepper with the seeds into his plate and politely offering the rest to the hosts: — Here, please, rub some on yourselves, heh, heh, heh, the Bulgarian way! No, no, rub it, listen to me and you’ll see what it’s like. Well, you know: beauty can’t be forced. Wait, let me rub mine so I can show you what’s called soup.

And indeed, Bay Ganyo had seasoned his soup to such a degree that an unaccustomed person would have poisoned himself on it. And he began to slurp; but when a Bulgarian slurps, he is no joke—three hundred dogs could be fighting and they still couldn’t drown him out. Large drops of sweat clouded his forehead and seemed about to pour into his plate. Bay Ganyo would slurp once from the tip of the spoon, put the spoon down, and stifle the fiery moisture with two or three bites of bread; then he would take up the spoon again, slurp some soup, sniff it inward through his nose, and again two or three bites of bread.

— Give me another little piece of bread. You’re eating quite without bread — Bay Ganyo wonders. — Give Bulgarians bread; we eat a lot of bread; not to boast, but with such soup, pardon me, with such soup I can eat a whole loaf of bread. I’ll bet on it.
They didn’t hold the bass, but even so Bay Ganyo destroyed quite a bit of bread.
— Where do you get this little wine from? — inquired Bay Ganyo, not because he was interested in the answer, but just to find an excuse for another glass.
— We’ll buy it — replies the owner, — is it good?

— Ah! Pure stuff! You’re buying it, eh? Hand me the bottle here. My stomach has been burning from the pepper like a heated iron; if I pour down the whole bottle now, it’ll sizzle inside. Ah, back home wine, half a lev an oka, and when you shine a little oka of it—there you are!... Ah, I burped, excuse me: that’s a bit vulgar, but pardon me, it’s human nature, you can’t hold it in!...

The lunch at Irechek’s, thanks to Bay Ganyo, turned out to be quite lively. They were served coffee in the reception room. Bay Ganyo, in gratitude for the tasty, and above all filling, lunch, wants to treat the host to a cigarette of tobacco, and, as fate would have it, the tobacco is in his saddlebags. To tell the truth, the tobacco pouch was in his pocket, but he had to find an excuse to go and check on the saddlebags; he cannot just leave his little perfume bottles with strangers like that—anything can happen in this world.
Bay Ganyo would not even hear of the host’s refusal to let him light up his tobacco: “How so, my dear fellow, can it be possible at all for a man not to smoke Bulgarian tobacco!”

Bay Ganyo fell silent and began to sip his coffee with relish. Now that’s what you call sipping!... To be in such a pleasant mood, to spend whole hours with a companion, to be in a room where no one will hear what you are saying, and even if they do hear it, they won’t understand you — under such favorable conditions, to hold back and not start talking politics is beyond Bay Ganyo’s strength. He could not restrain himself; he poured out his soul:

— Well, Bay Irechek, tell me, your honor, are you a Liberal or a Conservative? I suppose you’re a Conservative, as I see it. And I, if you ask me, can’t make heads or tails of either of them, but all right, let’s not offend them... You know, it’s all trade and bargaining, no joke... Shall I tell you the plain truth... (Might there be someone listening to us here?) Shall I tell you the plain truth? — Both of them are scoundrels!... Listen to me, and don’t be afraid! They’re all scoundrels, every last one of them!... But what can you do? You can’t kick against the pricks!... I’ve got little businesses, little enterprises, lawsuits in the courts — what can you do? If you’re not with them, you’re done for! And besides, don’t I want it myself — to be elected deputy, or mayor? There’s profit in such things. People have piled up money, do you know that? Fine, but if you don’t tip your hat to them — the devil himself couldn’t get you elected! That’s how it is! I’ve been through thick and thin in these matters, so I understand them...

Irechek could hardly have doubted that his guest understood “these matters.”
